story.heading: Clintons Testify in House Epstein Probe; Both Say They Had No Knowledge of Crimes
story.summary: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and former President Bill Clinton gave separate closed-door depositions to the Republican-led House Oversight Committee as part of its investigation into Jeffrey Epstein. Both said they had no knowledge of Epstein's or Ghislaine Maxwell's criminal activities; the sessions included a photo-leak disruption and drew partisan reactions.

segments.heading: Statements from Hillary and Bill Clinton
segments.text: Hillary Clinton told the House Oversight Committee that she "had no idea about their criminal activities" and did not recall ever meeting Jeffrey Epstein. Bill Clinton likewise told the panel he had no knowledge of Epstein's crimes and said his acquaintance with Epstein ended years before the criminal allegations surfaced. Both submitted opening statements and answered questions in multi-hour depositions.

Committee members from both parties questioned the Clintons as part of a wider probe into Epstein and Maxwell.

story.heading: Kansas invalidates transgender driver’s licenses and birth certificates; two men sue
story.summary: A new Kansas law that requires state documents to list sex assigned at birth has immediately invalidated previously changed driver’s licenses and birth certificates for transgender residents. About 1,700 people must obtain new licenses, and two transgender men filed a lawsuit the day the law took effect challenging its constitutionality while political leaders and advocates voiced competing views.

segments.heading: Provisions of the law and immediate effects
segments.text: The law bars any sex listing on driver’s licenses and birth certificates other than the one assigned at birth and invalidated existing records that did not comply. State officials notified affected residents that their credentials are invalid and must be replaced immediately. Reports estimate roughly 1,700 driver's licenses are affected; the vehicle division said there is no grace period and cited a $26 fee for obtaining a new standard license. The law also includes enforcement provisions for use of single-sex facilities and establishes civil and criminal penalties for violations by individuals and government entities.

segments.text: Two transgender men filed a lawsuit in Douglas County the same day the law took effect, arguing it violates rights to privacy, personal autonomy and due process under the state constitution and seeking to block the measure. The suit, filed by ACLU attorneys, says the law is discriminatory. The law was enacted after the Legislature overrode the governor’s veto; Gov. Laura Kelly criticized the measure as "poorly drafted" with "far-reaching consequences." Supporters in the Legislature said the measure protects girls and women and framed sex as determined at birth.

story.heading: Minnesota governor unveils anti-fraud measures after federal pause on Medicaid payments
story.summary: Federal officials announced a temporary withholding of $259.5 million in Medicaid payments to Minnesota pending a corrective action plan, prompting Governor Tim Walz to denounce the move and unveil state legislation aimed at strengthening fraud detection and enforcement. Authorities and state officials dispute the scope of alleged fraud and the potential impacts on residents.

segments.heading: Federal action: deferred Medicaid payments and conditions
segments.text: Federal officials announced they would withhold roughly $259.5 million in Medicaid payments to Minnesota and said the funds would be released only after the state implements a comprehensive corrective action plan. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said it gave the state 60 days to respond. Administration officials described the step as part of a broader effort to address alleged fraud in federal programs.

segments.heading: Walz response and state anti-fraud proposals
segments.text: Governor Tim Walz called the federal action "targeted retribution" and said it would harm Minnesotans who rely on Medicaid. He also unveiled a package of state legislation aimed at improving detection, oversight, investigative authority and penalties for fraud in public programs. Among the proposals is creation of a centralized Office of the Inspector General; the state Senate previously passed a bipartisan inspector general bill, but disagreements remain in the House over whether it should have law enforcement authority or focus on investigations.

story.heading: Federal judge allows Trump White House ballroom construction to continue, invites revised legal challenge
story.summary: A federal judge on Thursday denied a request from the National Trust for Historic Preservation to halt construction of a privately funded ballroom that replaced the White House East Wing, ruling the preservationists were unlikely to succeed under the legal theory presented while allowing them to amend their complaint.

segments.text: U.S. District Judge Richard Leon denied the preservation group's request for a temporary injunction, finding the National Trust for Historic Preservation was unlikely to succeed on the legal theory presented. The judge said the plaintiffs focused on the president's constitutional authority rather than the statutory basis that would be required to challenge the project under the Administrative Procedure Act, and noted the White House office overseeing the work is not an "agency" under the APA. He indicated the plaintiffs could amend their complaint to pursue the statutory claim and that he would consider such an amendment promptly.

story.heading: Federal prosecutors will not appeal ruling that bars death penalty in Luigi Mangione case
story.summary: Federal prosecutors informed a judge they will not seek an appeal of a decision that removed the federal murder charge that would have allowed capital punishment for Luigi Mangione in the December 2024 killing of UnitedHealth Group CEO Brian Thompson. The judge left stalking charges in place; Mangione faces a separate state murder trial.

segments.heading: Prosecutors decline to appeal; death penalty removed from federal case
segments.text: Deputy U.S. prosecutors told the court they will not ask the appeals court to overturn U.S. District Judge Margaret Garnett’s decision, which eliminated the federal charge that enabled a death-penalty request. That decision clears the way for a federal trial this fall while a state murder trial remains scheduled for earlier in the year.

citations.quote: federal prosecutors said Friday they wont appeal a judges ruling that bars them from seeking the death penalty against Luigi Mangione in the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson.
The death penalty is officially off the table for accused healthcare CEO killer Luigi Mangione.

segments.heading: Judge's legal reasoning and remaining federal charges
segments.text: Judge Garnett dismissed the federal murder count — charged as murder through use of a firearm — as legally flawed, and she also struck a gun charge. She left stalking counts in place. In her opinion she explained that to pursue the death penalty prosecutors needed to show the killing occurred while committing another "crime of violence," and she found stalking does not meet that definition. The judge cited Supreme Court precedent and related legal analysis in reaching that conclusion.

citations.quote: Garnett last month dismissed a federal murder charge  murder through use of a firearm  that had enabled prosecutors to seek capital punishment, finding it legally flawed.

"Over the course of the last two decades or so, the Supreme Court has embarked upon a legal journey, explained herein, that now requires lower courts to engage in an analysis totally divorced from the conduct at issue and centered on the hypothetically least serious conduct that the charged crime could possibly cover," she wrote.

segments.heading: Case timeline and background details
segments.text: Jury selection in the federal case is scheduled for Sept. 8, with opening statements and testimony to follow in October. A separate state murder trial is scheduled to begin in June. Mangione has pleaded not guilty in both federal and state proceedings. Authorities say surveillance video captured the December shooting and that writing was found on the ammunition; Mangione was arrested five days after the killing at a McDonalds in Altoona, Pennsylvania. His lawyers have argued public conduct around his arrest prejudiced the case.

story.heading: Pakistan and Afghanistan Exchange Strikes as Pakistani Minister Declares 'Open War'
story.summary: Fighting along the Pakistan-Afghanistan border escalated after cross-border attacks and airstrikes, with Pakistan's defence minister saying the country is in an "open war" and both sides issuing conflicting casualty and territorial claims. story.heading: Skiers Rescue Buried Man at Palisades Tahoe One Day After Deadly Castle Peak Avalanche
story.summary: Two skiers at Palisades Tahoe discovered and dug out a man who was buried in deep snow on Feb. 18, in an incident that occurred one day after an avalanche near Castle Peak killed nine backcountry skiers. Accounts of the rescue, the earlier avalanche and safety reminders were reported by multiple outlets.

segments.heading: Rescue at Palisades Tahoe
segments.text: On Feb. 18 two skiers at Palisades Tahoe (formerly Palisades Ski Resort) noticed the tips of a skiers skis protruding from deep snow and dug the person out. Video posted by one of the rescuers shows them uncovering the buried skier and making contact as they excavated large amounts of powder. The rescuer, identified in media reports as Carson Schmidt, described finding ski tips in a whiteout and said they moved immediately to dig the person out.

citations.quote: 'For whatever reason we just stop below, and I see ski tips and next thing you know, you just kind of go into go mode and just dig him out until you can find his face,' Schmidt told KCRA.
"For whatever reason we stopped and happened to just see tips of the skis in the whiteout and luckily we did," said Carson Schmidt, the person who posted the video.

segments.heading: Context: Castle Peak avalanche and regional fatalities
segments.text: The local rescue at Palisades Tahoe occurred one day after an avalanche on Feb. 17 near Castle Peak in Nevada County, adjacent to the Lake Tahoe region, that buried a group of backcountry skiers. Authorities reported nine people were killed in that avalanche and other recent incidents in the Lake Tahoe area resulted in additional fatalities. Some outlets described the Castle Peak event as among the deadliest backcountry disasters in California history and reported that it was the deadliest avalanche in the U.S. in decades.

citations.quote: Nine of the skiers, including six mothers on a trip and three ski guides, were killed by the snow slide, making it one of the deadliest backcountry disasters in California history.
This is the deadliest avalanche in the US in 45 years.

segments.heading: Uncertainty about the buried skier and safety reminders
segments.text: Reports say it is unclear how long the Palisades skier was buried, though the rescuer said there was about four feet of snow atop the person and that the individual eventually skied away from the scene. The rescuer and outlets framed the episode as a reminder to ski with a partner and carry appropriate safety equipment, and emphasized training and use of beacon, shovel and probe in deep-snow conditions.

citations.quote: 'He was in total shock, like all he wanted to find was his wife.'

'Everybody needs to be aware when you go out in that deep of snow. You need to ski with a partner, and you need to be trained. You need to have beacon, shovel, probe. You need to have all the right stuff.'
"Just want it to be a reminder to ski safe and ski with a buddy," Schmidt said in the post on social media.
It is unclear how long the man was buried or what happened to the man after he was rescued.

story.heading: NASA's Artemis II preparation: fueling test, technical issues and why hydrogen complicates launches
story.summary: NASA prepared for the crewed Artemis II mission with a recent fueling test and astronaut quarantines, but engineers reported new hardware issues that prompted plans to roll the Space Launch System (SLS) back to the Vehicle Assembly Building and removed an early March launch target. Engineers are investigating helium and hydrogen system problems; experts say hydrogen's physical properties offer performance benefits but make containment challenging.

segments.heading: Planned launch and crew preparations
segments.text: Agency statements and media reports indicated that a recent fueling test of the SLS rocket prompted NASA to target an early March launch for Artemis II and that the four crew members entered pre-flight quarantine. The Artemis II crew includes commander Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, mission specialist Christina Koch and Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen. The test and crew preparations were presented as steps toward a crewed lunar flyby.

citations.quote: NASA announced that it successfully conducted a fueling test of the powerful SLS rocket, and with that, it’s aiming to launch the Artemis II mission in two weeks, on March 6.

segments.heading: New hardware problem and schedule impact
segments.text: After the fueling test, engineers detected an interruption in helium flow to the SLS interim cryogenic propulsion stage. NASA stated it would prepare to roll the vehicle back to the Vehicle Assembly Building for further inspection and repair, and said that action removed the March launch window from consideration; the agency identified early April as the next available opportunity. Officials described several possible causes under review, including filter, umbilical interface or check-valve issues observed in previous preparations.

segments.heading: Why hydrogen fuel presents recurring challenges
segments.text: Recent pre-launch tests also highlighted liquid hydrogen leaks during a wet dress rehearsal earlier in February, a safety concern because hydrogen is easily ignited and difficult to contain. Engineers and analysts note that hydrogen continues to be used because its low molecular weight gives it a high specific impulse, improving rocket performance despite handling difficulties. NASA and contractors continue troubleshooting valves, umbilicals and filters that can permit hydrogen or related system problems to recur.
